**The Weight of a Single Word**

There’s a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. The air is thick with the kind of silence that isn’t absence but presence—an almost tangible thing, like the hum of a tuning fork before the first note. I’ve always loved that moment. It’s the only time I feel like I’m not just *in* the world but *part* of it, a temporary stitch in the fabric of something vast and unknowable.

Words have weight. Not just the ones we speak, but the ones we swallow, the ones that sit heavy in the chest like stones in a pocket. I’ve carried a lot of them over the years—some sharp, some smooth, some so heavy I could swear they left bruises. And yet, for all their weight, words are also the lightest things we have. They vanish the moment they’re spoken, dissolving into the air like sugar in water. You can’t hold them. You can’t take them back. Once they’re out, they belong to the world, and the world does with them what it will.

I wonder sometimes if that’s why we’re so afraid of them.

---

I was twelve the first time I learned how powerful a single word could be. It was a Tuesday, or maybe a Wednesday—those days blur together when you’re young, when every day feels like a lifetime and a second all at once. I was in the schoolyard, perched on the edge of the jungle gym, watching the other kids play some game that involved a lot of shouting and very little actual rules. I wasn’t part of it. I never was. I was the kind of kid who hovered at the edges, the one who noticed things—the way the light hit the pavement at a certain angle, the way the wind carried the scent of rain before the clouds even appeared, the way some people’s laughter sounded like breaking glass.

Then he said it.

*Freak.*

Just that. One word. Four letters. It shouldn’t have been enough to knock the breath out of me, but it did. It wasn’t even directed at me, not really. It was thrown at someone else, some poor kid who’d tripped over his own feet and sent a soccer ball flying into the wrong goal. But it landed on me anyway, like a stone skipping across water, each ripple hitting me in turn. *Freak. Freak. Freak.*

I didn’t know then that words could be weapons. I didn’t know they could carve you open and leave you bleeding without ever touching your skin. I didn’t know that some wounds never close, that some scars don’t fade, that some words echo in the hollows of your bones long after the person who spoke them has forgotten they ever existed.

I do now.

---

There’s a difference between *hearing* and *listening*. Most people hear. They let words wash over them, let them slip in one ear and out the other like water through cupped hands. But listening—*real* listening—is different. It’s an act of vulnerability. It’s saying, *I see you. I hear you. Your words matter.* And that’s terrifying, because if you let someone’s words matter, then you have to let *them* matter too.

I’ve spent most of my life not listening. Not because I didn’t want to, but because I was afraid. Afraid of what I might hear. Afraid of what it might mean. Afraid of the weight of it all.

But then there are the moments when you can’t *not* listen. When the words hit you like a physical force, when they rearrange something inside you, when they make you see the world—or yourself—in a way you never have before.

Like the time my grandmother told me, *You don’t have to be strong all the time.* I was sixteen, and I’d spent years building walls so high and so thick I’d forgotten what it was like to feel anything but the weight of them. That one sentence—soft, quiet, almost lost in the hum of the refrigerator—cracked something open in me. It wasn’t a grand revelation. It wasn’t a thunderbolt from the heavens. It was just… a word. A permission. A reminder that I didn’t have to carry everything alone.

Or the time my best friend, in the middle of a breakdown I didn’t know how to fix, whispered, *I’m not okay.* Not *I’m fine.* Not *It’s nothing.* Just *I’m not okay.* And in that moment, I realized that sometimes the bravest thing you can do is admit that you’re not brave at all.

---

I’ve been thinking a lot about silence lately. Not the kind that comes before dawn, but the kind that settles between people when words fail. The kind that stretches and stretches until it feels like it might swallow you whole. I used to think silence was the absence of something, but now I know it’s just another kind of language. A language of things left unsaid, of emotions too big for words, of truths that can’t be spoken because they’re too raw, too real.

There’s a quote I love—*The deepest wounds aren’t made by sharp words, but by the absence of them.* I don’t know who said it, but it haunts me. Because it’s true. There’s a violence in silence, in the way it can make you feel like you don’t exist. Like you’re screaming into a void and no one—not even the void—is listening.

I’ve been on both sides of that silence. I’ve been the one who couldn’t find the words, who let the moment pass because I was too afraid to speak. And I’ve been the one left waiting, wondering if I was ever heard at all.

---

I don’t know if words can change the world. I don’t know if they can heal the broken places inside us, or bridge the gaps between people, or make sense of the chaos. But I do know this: they matter. Even the small ones. Even the ones we don’t mean. Even the ones we wish we could take back.

Because words are how we reach for each other. They’re how we say *I’m here* and *I see you* and *You’re not alone.* And sometimes, that’s enough.

Sometimes, it has to be.
